title: The blessing
hook: the service ends in a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offering: a basket on a pole, bread carried up the aisle, and David handing back what was handed to him. Your line was all things come of thee. Did the gift you chose leave your hands? Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

Coats are half on. The last hymn is over. A toddler is already making a break for the door, and someone at the end of the row is checking a phone. Then the minister raises a hand over the room, or both hands, palms out, and the shuffling stops. Heads bow. And into the quiet come words from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." A few more lines, an amen, and then the doors open onto the parking lot and the rest of the week. Before anyone reaches the car, something has been spoken over them. Today's word is benediction.

A benediction is a blessing spoken over people, and a service often closes with one. One often used comes from Numbers. God tells Moses to speak to Aaron and his sons: "On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel." And then the words, in the King James Bible: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Three lines, and each one reaches a little further: kept, then shone upon, then given peace. These were Israel's words first, and Jews pray them still. Now notice who is doing the blessing. The very next verse says the priests "shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The person with the raised hands passes the blessing on. In the text, God is the one who blesses. Then the hands. In Leviticus, after the offerings, "Aaron lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them." And near the end of Luke's Gospel, there are raised hands too. Out near Bethany, Jesus "lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them." In Luke, the disciples' last sight of him is a blessing in progress. Churches end in different ways. Some use Numbers. Some use Paul's line, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Some add the sign of the cross. And then, often, a few last words, like these: go in peace. A raised hand, and the room empties into the week.

Here's the practice: bless someone. Settle, and breathe. Lift one hand a little, palm out, the way a minister does over a room. Let it rest in the air toward one person heading into a hard day: a friend before a test, a parent in a hospital, a coworker who's stretched thin. If you pray, you can say the old words over them, slowly, one line per breath: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee. The LORD make his face shine upon thee. The LORD give thee peace. If you don't pray, wish them those three things in your own way: that they're kept safe, that someone looks on them kindly, that they find some peace. The bell holds the time.
Benediction. A blessing spoken over people, often at the end of a service, often the words from Numbers, spoken as people leave.
Your line: go in peace. Today, when someone leaves, at the door, at the end of a call, don't just say bye. Send them off with one good word. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Christian services often end with a benediction: the minister or priest raises a hand or both hands over the congregation and speaks a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26 or 2 Corinthians 13:14, sometimes with the sign of the cross, followed by a dismissal such as "go in peace."

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples near Bethany, near the end of Luke's Gospel. Jesus is about to be parted from you. what is he doing?
options: lifting up his hands and blessing you.
giving instructions for building a church.
fork.reveal: "he lifted up his hands, and blessed them." in Luke, the last thing the disciples see is a blessing still under way.

original.note: Hebrew: may he bless thee, the first word of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: the benediction is the signal that church is over.
what it means: a blessing spoken over the people as they're sent out, often the three lines from Numbers.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 6:27. the priests "put my name" on the people, and God says "I will bless them": the speaker passes it on.

notes: First day of a new week (1345–1351).
'Many services close with one' — the outline says often Numbers 6:24–26; the teach says one often used.
'Jews pray them still' — brief neighbor mention (the Birkat Kohanim); confirm wording.
'Go in peace' as a dismissal: one of the Roman Missal's options; Orthodox 'Let us go forth in peace'. Stated generally ('in words like these'); confirm.
Original: יְבָרֶכְךָ (yevarekhekha), first word of Numbers 6:24; confirm pointing and transliteration.
Audit pass: stress in the original's 'say' moved to the final syllable (the -kha suffix carries the accent: yevarekhekhá); confirm against a Hebrew reader.

Editor pass: hook reordered so it doesn't open like day 1342's; 'the service doesn't just stop' and 'points out the door' cut as a repeat of day 1337's sending angle; 'many services' softened; practice now begins with a raised hand rather than another 'bring a face to mind' opening.
